extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in history, philosophy, and practice of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for mathematical practice: how to choose and use symbols and notation, when and how to abstract and idealize models, standards for proofs (existence/uniqueness), and historical/technical requirements for applied practices (e.g., astrology as practiced historically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genethlialogy requirements (astrological natal charts)
rubrics_metrics.description: To predict the course of one's life via genethlialogy one needs the exact moment and place of birth and must calculate planetary positions and relations (such as conjunctions and oppositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses almanacs to determine planetary states at birth; accuracy of birth time/place directly affects forecast quality. Example: practitioners relied on exact time/place for accurate natal charts; without exact data predictions are only approximate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catarchic astrology requirement (timing acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Catarchic astrology asserts any act is influenced by celestial omens at the moment of its inception; forecasting auspicious dates requires knowledge of future planetary positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To pick auspicious dates, compute future planetary positions and their relations. Implies need for predictive astronomy and accurate ephemerides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatory astrology principle (moment-of-question matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrogatory astrology holds that the moment at which a question is asked affects the correctness of the astrological answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies that timing (the instant of interrogation) is an essential input variable; accurate practice requires noting exact time of question as part of data for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical requirements for intensive astrological practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensive astrology necessitated knowledge of astronomy, mathematics, medicine, accurate planetary tables, precise instruments, accurate clocks, and reliable computational methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice distinguished between approximate (low-cost) horoscopes and exact (higher-cost) horoscopes; nobles or clergy demanded first-order accuracy leading to investment in better tables/instruments. Anti-pattern: performing intensive astrological prescriptions without precise input data or reliable instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model validity criterion (astrology as a scientific model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful scientific model must give a correct account of reality; astrology ultimately failed because it provided a wrong model of reality despite mathematical elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: even mathematically elaborate theories can be disconfirmed if their underlying model is incorrect. Use empirical adequacy as a criterion for model acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as a vehicle toward the infinite / religious analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics, seen as the science of the infinite and of deductive structure, can be experienced as bringing the mind closer to the divine; mathematical certainty and stringency are contrasted with religious faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate cultural or philosophical claims about mathematics' status: when judging rhetoric about mathematics as 'religion' or quasi-religious, consider the role of proof, shared concepts, and consensus among practitioners as distinguishing features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus and finality via proof
rubrics_metrics.description: If a mathematical question has a definite answer, different mathematicians using different methods and in different centuries should find the same answer; proof provides finality and universal acceptance among adherents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical claims, inspect whether a proof provides definitive resolution; the presence of rigorous proof is a key criterion for mathematical agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence theorems as essential standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics one requires existence theorems to guarantee that problems posed under given a priori restrictions actually have solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building or judging a mathematical theory, check that existence results have been established; absence of existence theorems is a serious lacuna. Example: many problems are posed which demonstrably have no solutions unless existence is proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness theorems as essential standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniqueness theorems assert that, under given conditions, a problem has at most one solution; mathematicians prize uniqueness because it yields a well-determined, predictable situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories for whether uniqueness (or classification up to natural equivalence) has been addressed; lack of uniqueness can indicate ambiguity needing resolution or the creation of quotient constructions to restore uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of proof techniques (e.g., contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard mathematical proof techniques, such as proof by contradiction, are legitimate and useful tools for demonstrating existence, uniqueness, or impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing proofs, consider whether appropriate techniques have been used and whether their application is logically sound. Historical examples: theological proofs sometimes resemble mathematical proof-by-contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction via idealization (modeling assumptions must be explicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction/idealization strips away accidental sensible properties to form ideal mathematical objects (e.g., ideal straight line); mathematical models must state their simplifying assumptions explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a model, check the explicit list of assumptions (example: the vibrating string assumptions: perfectly flexible, constant density, small displacements, motion confined to a plane, no external forces). Anti-pattern: hiding or failing to state key idealizing assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance: do not over-abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: While abstraction is powerful and necessary, excessive or ultra-abstract programs can become incomprehensible, uninteresting, or unable to regenerate new ideas; motivation usually comes from coarse/concrete problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge abstract theories by their intelligibility, motivational roots, and ability to connect back to motivating problems. Warning: ultra-abstract work that mainly straightens terminology and reestablishes known results may be of limited value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction should be supplemented by concreteness/emotion where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly abstract accounts (e.g., of God) require bolstering from concrete metaphors or emotional practice; pure abstraction alone can leave too little to affirm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exposition and pedagogy, complement abstract definitions/theorems with concrete examples, diagrams, and metaphors to aid understanding and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal functions of mathematical symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols in mathematics principally serve to (1) designate with precision and clarity and (2) abbreviate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating notation, ask whether it aids precise designation and useful abbreviation. Example: good notation frees cognitive effort for higher-level reasoning (Whitehead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and unambiguity of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of each symbol or symbol string must be razor sharp and unambiguous; symbol perception must distinguish it from other symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether symbol definitions are explicit and unambiguous; committees have attempted standardization but organic growth prevails. Anti-pattern: introducing symbols whose meaning overlaps or conflicts with established symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual roles of symbols: calculation vs interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical symbols are used both for calculation (transformations verifiable, machine-like) and for interpretation (associating symbols with concepts), and these roles impose different precision requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design notation so that calculation rules are precise and implementable (ideally machine-verifiable), while recognizing interpretation relies on human communication and shared concepts. When judging notation, evaluate both aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation should suggest fruitful generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Good notation can suggest natural extensions and new concepts (e.g., Leibniz's D notation hints at fractional/negative differentiation leading to operational calculus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing or evaluating notation, prefer forms that make plausible generalizations manifest and encourage further development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic constraint on symbol invention and standardization
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of new symbols faces practical barriers (need for widespread acceptance, typesetting costs); there is a survival-of-the-fittest dynamic among symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before introducing new notation, consider adoption likelihood, reproducibility (typesetting/printing), and whether existing symbols suffice. Anti-pattern: inventing idiosyncratic symbols without community uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with heavy abbreviation in formal systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations and compounded definitions in formal logic make statements compact but expanding them into primitive atomic form can produce extremely long, error-prone strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance concision with readability and verifiability; when formal definitions are deeply nested, provide expansion guidance or modular explanations to avoid unreadable expansions.
